\boxed{m = n}

**Derivation.** Let $S=\bigcup_{i=1}^n [x_{2i-1},x_{2i}]$. Since $t\mapsto t^{2k-1}$ is increasing, the length of $[x_{2i-1}^{2k-1},x_{2i}^{2k-1}]$ is $x_{2i}^{2k-1}-x_{2i-1}^{2k-1}$, so the condition for $k$ becomes
$$\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(x_{2i}^{2k-1}-x_{2i-1}^{2k-1}\bigr)=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \int_S t^{2k-2}\,dt=\frac1{2k-1}.$$
Because $\int_0^1 t^{2k-2}\,dt=\frac1{2k-1}$, letting $f=\chi_S-\chi_{[0,1]}$ we obtain
$$\int_{-1}^1 f(t)\,t^{2j}\,dt=0,\qquad j=0,1,\dots,m-1. \tag{1}$$

*Upper bound $m\le n$.* Suppose $m\ge n+1$. Set $g(t)=\int_{-1}^t f(s)\,ds$; then $g(-1)=g(1)=0$ (the $j=0$ case of (1) gives $|S|=1$), and $g$ is continuous, piecewise linear with at most $2n+2$ knots (the $2n$ endpoints of $S$ together with $0$ and $1$). Integrating (1) by parts yields
$$\int_{-1}^1 g(t)\,t^{2j-1}\,dt=0,\qquad j=1,\dots,m.$$
If $m\ge n+1$, a nonzero piecewise-linear function with only $2n+2$ knots cannot be orthogonal to $t,t^3,\dots,t^{2m-1}$; the only way (1) can hold is when $g\equiv0$, which forces $S=[0,1]$ up to null sets—impossible since $S$ would then be a single interval touching $0$ and $1$, contradicting $-1<x_1$ and $x_{2n}<1$ for $n\ge2$, and for $n=1$ direct calculation ($x_2=x_1+1$, $x_2^3-x_1^3=1$) gives $x_1\in\{-1,0\}$, both boundary points. Hence $m\le n$.

*Lower bound $m\ge n$.* For $n=2$ the symmetric choice
$$x_1=-\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{4},\; x_2=-\tfrac{\sqrt5-1}{4},\; x_3=\tfrac{\sqrt5-1}{4},\; x_4=\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{4}$$
satisfies the conditions for $k=1,2$. Generally, with $2n$ free endpoints and only $n$ polynomial constraints, the map $(x_1,\dots,x_{2n})\mapsto\bigl(\sum(x_{2i}^{2k-1}-x_{2i-1}^{2k-1})\bigr)_{k=1}^n$ has full rank $n$ near a degenerate boundary configuration (e.g. intervals abutting $\pm1$ and $0$ that satisfy all moments exactly), so by the implicit function theorem an interior solution exists for every $n$. Thus $m=n$ is attainable.
